content.text: React treats your component as a calculation: same props, state and context in, same JSX out, and nothing outside it changes. It relies on that to render twice in development, restart a render, skip one or run it on the server. Side effects in the component body break the moment any of that happens, even when the screen looks right.
The growth team's dashboard says the average visitor views each product page several times per visit, and nobody believes it. The cause is one line at the top of

. It sits in the component body, so every re-render counts as a view: picking a size, changing the quantity, a price refresh. In development every view was logged twice, and the team had shrugged that off as React being strange in dev mode.
The belief: the component body is just code that runs when the component shows up. If the UI looks right, then a log call, a counter or an analytics event in there is harmless.
It's an understandable belief. A function component's body reads like a script that runs "on show", the same way a constructor or an old

did. In a simple app, each update usually renders once, so the side effect seems to fire at the right moment. And there's a true part: React doesn't demand purity in the strict mathematical sense. Its rules say it doesn't mind small impurities, as long as calling the component several times is safe and doesn't affect the rendering of other components. Analytics, DOM writes and changed outside variables fail exactly that test.

React's docs define a pure component with two rules. It minds its own business: it doesn't change objects or variables that existed before it was called. And same inputs, same output: given the same props, state and context, it returns the same JSX. A
is anything else your code does that someone can observe: a network request, a write to the DOM or to
, a change to a variable outside the component.
React may run render more or fewer times than you think
Because React assumes every component is a
, it feels free to call it whenever that helps:

items.text: As the earlier articles in this path showed, a state change, a parent's render or a context update runs the body again, even when nothing the user sees has changed.
Strict Mode calls your component body, state initializers, updaters and
functions twice to expose impure code. Production builds skip this.
If data changes in the middle of rendering a deep tree, React can restart and discard the unfinished render. A side effect inside it already happened anyway.
and React Compiler skip renders whose inputs haven't changed, which is only safe because pure output can be cached. A side effect there silently doesn't run.

content.text: So the number of renders says nothing about how many times the user saw something. Anything that must happen a specific number of times can't live in render.
React gives you two places that run outside render.
come first: they run because the user did something, they're never called during render, and they don't need to be pure.

run after React commits, to synchronize with a system outside React, and the docs call them the last resort when no event fits. "The product page is now on screen" is one of those cases: there's no click, so the view event belongs in an Effect keyed on the product.

blocks.title: Two view events locally is expected

content.text: Strict Mode also runs every Effect an extra time in development, to check that it cleans up after itself. Seeing the view event twice on your machine is that check, not a bug; production builds don't do it.
The other half of purity is not mutating inputs. A classic slip is sorting props during render:

changes the array the parent owns, so the parent's own list, and every other component sharing that array, silently changes order. Creating an object or array during render and then mutating it is fine, though; React's docs call that local mutation, and nobody outside can tell.

blocks.title: Don't switch off Strict Mode to hide the doubles

content.text: A doubled log or a list item that appears twice in development is Strict Mode doing its job. The same code misbehaves in production too, on every ordinary re-render, just less visibly. Fix the component, not the check.
How to apply it in your project
rule flags known impure calls during render,
and treat anything that appears twice in development as a bug report about render.

items.title: Audit component bodies for calls that leave the component

content.text: Look for requests, analytics, timers, storage and DOM access at the top level of components. Move each one to the event handler that caused it, or to an Effect if it syncs with what's on screen.
or assign fields on props, state or context. Use
, spread or a local copy instead.

items.text: A pure component returns the same JSX for the same props, state and context, and changes nothing that existed before it ran.
React may render twice, restart, skip or move a render to the server, so render count isn't a measure of anything.
Side effects belong in event handlers first, and in Effects when they sync with something outside React.
Local mutation is fine; mutating props, state or outside variables is not, and Strict Mode plus the lints catch it.
